name: Exosome serums
lead: Exosome serums are skincare and post-procedure products marketed as containing exosomes or other extracellular vesicles, tiny membrane-bound particles that cells release to carry proteins, lipids and RNA to other cells [1][2]. They are promoted for skin rejuvenation: smoother texture, fewer fine lines and wrinkles, a brighter, more even tone, and faster recovery after treatments such as microneedling. The idea is that the vesicles deliver signals that nudge skin cells toward repair.

Beauty media has covered them as a trend; Elle published a 2026 roundup titled 'The Best Exosome Face Serums of 2026 for Younger, Smoother Skin, According to Experts' [3]. Clinics often pair exosome products with microneedling or radiofrequency microneedling, and a completed 30-participant study registered in 2024 tested AnteAGE Biosomes with radiofrequency microneedling for facial rejuvenation [4].

Exosomes are an active research area in medicine, but the US Food and Drug Administration stated in December 2019 that there are no FDA-approved exosome products, and that exosomes used to treat disease are regulated as drugs and biological products [5]. Wikipedia reports that some clinics sell exosomes in skincare products with 'cosmetic' labelling, and that the FDA maintains cosmetic uses also require formal review [2].

paras: Extracellular vesicles are released by nearly all cell types; most are under about 200 nm. Some bud from the cell surface, while exosomes form inside cells and are released when multivesicular bodies fuse with the membrane. They can carry proteins, lipids, RNA and other molecules, and are thought to pass signals between cells [1].

Exosomes were identified in maturing reticulocytes in 1983 by groups led by Stahl and by Johnstone, and Johnstone's group named them exosomes in 1987 [2]. Wikipedia says it is unclear whether exosomes differ meaningfully from other extracellular vesicles [2]. Its overview also lists proposed risks of vesicles in biology, including effects on clotting and the spread of inflammation, and notes that tumor-derived vesicles can promote cancer invasion; these concern vesicles in the body rather than cosmetic products specifically [1].

Exosome products are sold as serums and as treatments used after procedures. Wikipedia says some clinics sell exosomes in skincare products, claiming benefits such as wrinkle reduction, using cosmetic labelling [2]. Exosomes from oral keratinocytes accelerated wound healing in rats, an animal finding that is cited as background for the skin-repair idea [2].

On December 6, 2019 the FDA stated that there are no FDA-approved exosome products and that exosomes used to treat diseases in humans are regulated as drugs and biological products requiring premarket review [5]. It said it was aware of multiple reports of serious adverse events in Nebraska patients treated with unapproved products marketed as containing exosomes, and that some clinics offer exosome products with unsubstantiated claims [5]. It asked professionals and consumers to report adverse events through MedWatch [5]. Wikipedia reports that the FDA cautioned several firms about exosome marketing in 2020 [2].
Standardisation remains a major gap in vesicle science, and contamination by non-vesicle material has been a persistent problem in isolation [1].

Few trials appear in registries. One completed 30-participant study registered in 2024 tested AnteAGE Biosomes with radiofrequency microneedling for facial rejuvenation, with skin aging, wrinkles and skin tone as listed conditions; no results are given in the registration entry [4]. A separate registered phase 2 acne trial concerns skin microbiome balance and has no published results [6]. No published efficacy results for exosome serums were found.

card.summary: Vesicle-based regeneration serums with promising biology but almost no published human skin data.
card.note: Product composition is hard to standardize; no published efficacy results found.

quick.overview:
Exosome serums contain extracellular vesicles, tiny particles cells release to signal each other, and are marketed for skin regeneration, often with microneedling.

Only a couple of registered trials turned up, and no published results for cosmetic use.
quick.mechanism: Vesicles carry proteins, lipids and RNA between cells; the idea behind the products is that these signals could influence skin cells. This has not been shown for the products in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Vesicle science has persistent standardization and contamination problems. No regulatory or adverse-event data for cosmetic products were in the sources reviewed.

chain: Serum or post-procedure product applied to the skin, often after microneedling
Vesicles are proposed to carry growth and repair signals to skin cells
Proponents expect smoother, more even, younger-looking skin and quicker recovery
angle.text: Marketers and clinics describe exosome products as delivering cell-signalling cargo that supports collagen, skin repair and glow, and use them alongside microneedling or laser treatments for facial rejuvenation. The effect on skin is what the products claim.
